title: Medicare rules and costs for people age 65 who are still working
主要内容: Medicare rules and costs for individuals aged 65 who are still working are important considerations for those nearing retirement. The share of people aged 65 to 74 in the workforce is projected to reach 30.2% in 2026, up from 26.8% in 2016 and 17.5% in 1996. Individuals working for companies with more than 20 employees have the choice to either continue their group health insurance or enroll in Medicare. If they delay enrollment, they must be aware of deadlines related to losing coverage at work, such as retirement. Medicare enrollment season brings fierce competition among insurers to attract baby boomers. Original Medicare includes Part A (hospital coverage) and Part B (outpatient and medical equipment coverage). A seven-month window is available to sign up, starting three months before the 65th birthday month and ending three months after. Late-enrollment penalties apply if not signed up when eligible and no exceptions are met. Qualifying insurance, such as a group plan through a large employer, is an exception. Part A is free with a 10-year work history, while Part B has a standard monthly premium of $144.60 for 2020, with higher-income filers paying more. Standalone Part D plans average $30 monthly, with higher-income enrollees paying more. Roughly a third of Medicare enrollees choose Advantage Plans, which include Part D and extras like dental and vision. Medigap policies, which cover copays and co-insurance, range from $126 to $464 monthly for a 65-year-old male. For individuals aged 65 who are still working, Medicare rules and costs can be complex. The cost of Medicare varies, with premiums for 65-year-old women ranging from $118 to $464. When comparing options, it's essential to consider the cost of coverage, potential use of the healthcare system, and prescription drug expenses. Workers at companies with at least 20 employees can delay enrolling in Medicare until they lose their group insurance, typically upon retirement. However, Danielle Roberts, co-founder of Boomer Benefits, suggests that current employer insurance may be more cost-effective due to lower premiums and other cost-sharing aspects. If Part A is free, individuals can enroll without affecting their health savings account. Medicare might be preferable if frequent therapy visits or specialty drugs are involved. For those with small employers, Medicare enrollment is mandatory, and it's often more cost-effective to drop employer coverage and opt for Medigap or Advantage Plans. The average premium for single coverage through employer-sponsored health insurance is $7,188, with employees contributing an average of $1,242.
